questions.q: What is the SI unit of pressure?
questions.a: Newton per square metre (N/m2), also called the pascal
o: Newton per square metre (N/m2), also called the pascal
Newton (N), which is the same unit as for force
Square metre (m2), the same unit as area
Newton multiplied by square metre (N m2)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A school bag with broad straps feels more comfortable on the shoulders than an equally heavy bag with narrow straps.
Reason (R): Broad straps spread the same weight over a larger area of the shoulders, so the pressure on them is less.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Define pressure. (b) A box pushes straight down on a floor with a force of 60 N over an area of 3 m2. Find the pressure it exerts on the floor.
questions.a: (a) Pressure is the force acting per unit area (Pressure = Force / Area). (b) Pressure = 60 N / 3 m2 = 20 N/m2, that is 20 Pa.
s: Defines pressure as force per unit area
Divides 60 N by 3 m2 to get 20 N/m2 (20 Pa)

questions.q: True or False? 'If the same force is spread over twice the area, the pressure becomes half.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Pressure = Force / Area, so when the force stays the same and the area is doubled, the pressure is halved.
s: States True
Explains using Pressure = Force / Area that doubling the area with the same force halves the pressure

questions.q: Give one reason for each. (a) A vegetable seller places a round piece of cloth under the basket on her head. (b) A bucket of water is easier to lift by a broad handle than by a narrow one. (c) An iron nail is driven into wood with its pointed end, not its head.
questions.a: (a) The cloth increases the area over which the weight acts, so the pressure on her head is less. (b) The broad handle spreads the weight over a larger area of the hand, reducing the pressure. (c) The pointed end has a very small area, so the same force gives a much larger pressure, which drives the nail in easily.
s: (a) Cloth increases the area under the load, so the pressure on the head is reduced
(b) Broad handle spreads the weight over a larger area, so less pressure on the hand
(c) Pointed end has a small area, so the pressure is larger and the nail goes in easily

questions.q: Answer each part in one or two lines. (a) Write the formula for pressure. (b) Write the SI unit of pressure and its other name. (c) A crate of books presses down on a table with a force of 150 N over an area of 0.5 m2. Find the pressure. (d) The same crate is placed on a face whose area is 1 m2. What is the pressure now? (e) Give one example from daily life where the area is made larger to reduce the pressure.
questions.a: (a) Pressure = Force / Area. (b) N/m2, also called the pascal (Pa). (c) 150 N / 0.5 m2 = 300 Pa. (d) 150 N / 1 m2 = 150 Pa, half the earlier pressure. (e) Any one: broad straps on a school bag, a broad handle on a bucket, a round piece of cloth under a head load.
s: (a) Writes Pressure = Force / Area
(b) Gives N/m2 and names it the pascal (Pa)
(c) Calculates 150 / 0.5 = 300 Pa
(d) Calculates 150 / 1 = 150 Pa
(e) Gives a correct example such as broad bag straps, a broad bucket handle or a cloth pad under a head load

questions.q: Four loads rest on a sand tray, each pressing straight down. Which one puts the greatest pressure on the sand?
questions.a: A 90 N load on 0.2 m2
o: A 90 N load on 0.2 m2
A 120 N load on 0.4 m2
A 200 N load on 0.8 m2
A 60 N load on 0.15 m2

questions.q:
Read these statements about pressure.
I. A pressure of 1 Pa means a force of 1 N acting at right angles on an area of 1 m2.
II. When the same force acts on a larger area, the pressure becomes larger.
III. A force of 40 N acting on an area of 0.5 m2 gives a pressure of 80 Pa.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: Tsering weighs 480 N. On fresh snow in Ladakh, her ordinary shoes touch the snow over a total area of 0.03 m2. When she wears a pair of flat snow-boards, the area becomes 0.24 m2. (a) Find the pressure on the snow with ordinary shoes. (b) Find the pressure with the snow-boards. (c) How many times smaller is the pressure with the snow-boards, and why does she sink less?
questions.a: (a) 480 N / 0.03 m2 = 16000 Pa. (b) 480 N / 0.24 m2 = 2000 Pa. (c) 16000 / 2000 = 8, so the pressure is 8 times smaller. Her weight is the same, but it is spread over a larger area, so the pressure on the snow is less and she sinks less.
s: (a) Calculates 16000 Pa
(b) Calculates 2000 Pa
(c) Finds 8 times and explains that the same weight over a larger area gives less pressure

questions.q:
For a craft fair in Guwahati, the organisers must place a display stand on the school lawn. The stand and its goods weigh 2400 N. The gardener warns that the grass gets crushed if the pressure on it is more than 8000 Pa. The stand can be used on its four legs, each touching the ground over 0.02 m2, or on a flat wooden base plate of area 0.5 m2.
(a) Find the pressure on the grass when the stand rests on its four legs.
(b) Find the pressure when it rests on the base plate.
(c) Which way should the stand be placed to save the grass? Give a reason.
(d) A seller wants to add 1200 N more goods to the stand on its base plate. Will the grass still be safe? What is the largest extra load the base plate stand can take?
questions.a: (a) Total leg area = 4 x 0.02 = 0.08 m2, so pressure = 2400 / 0.08 = 30000 Pa. (b) 2400 / 0.5 = 4800 Pa. (c) On the base plate: 4800 Pa is below the 8000 Pa limit, while 30000 Pa on the legs is far above it, because the larger area spreads the same weight. (d) Yes: 3600 / 0.5 = 7200 Pa, still below 8000 Pa. The largest total load is 8000 x 0.5 = 4000 N, so the largest extra load is 4000 - 2400 = 1600 N.
s: (a) Adds the leg areas to 0.08 m2 and finds 30000 Pa
(b) Finds 4800 Pa
(c) Chooses the base plate, comparing both pressures with 8000 Pa
(d) Finds 7200 Pa (safe) and the largest extra load of 1600 N

questions.q: Why are overhead water tanks placed at a height?
questions.a: A taller water column gives more pressure at the taps, so water flows well.
o: A taller water column gives more pressure at the taps, so water flows well.
A tank kept high can hold a larger amount of water than one kept on the ground.
Water kept at a height becomes lighter, so it flows down the pipes more easily.
A greater weight of water then rests on each tap, whatever the height of the column.

questions.q: In which directions does a liquid in a container exert pressure?
questions.a: In all directions, including on the sides of the container
o: In all directions, including on the sides of the container
Only downwards, on the bottom of the container that holds it
Only sideways, on the walls of the container
Only upwards, towards the surface of the liquid

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The base of a dam is made much broader than its top.
Reason (R): The water stored in a dam presses sideways on its wall, and this pressure is very large near the bottom.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: State two observations which show that water exerts pressure on the sides (walls) of a container or a pipe.
questions.a: (1) When small holes are made around the sides of a plastic bottle filled with water, water flows out through the side holes. (2) Water spurts out like a fountain from a leaking joint or hole in a water pipe.
s: Water flows out of holes made in the sides of a filled bottle
Water spurts out like a fountain from a leak or hole in a water pipe

questions.q: True or False? 'The water in a full glass pushes on the sides of the glass as well as on its bottom.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Liquids exert pressure not only on the bottom of a container but also on its sides; in fact they exert pressure in all directions, which is why water flows out of holes in the side of a bottle.
s: States True
Explains that liquids exert pressure in all directions, shown by water flowing out of side holes

questions.q: Use what you know about liquid pressure to explain each of these in one or two lines. (a) A balloon tied below a water-filled pipe bulges more when more water is poured into the pipe. (b) Water spurts out like a fountain from a small hole in a water pipe. (c) The base of a dam is built broader than its top. (d) In a three-storeyed house with a tank on the roof, the tap on the ground floor gives a stronger stream than the tap on the top floor.
questions.a: (a) The height of the water column increases, so the pressure at the bottom of the pipe increases and the balloon bulges more. (b) Water presses on the walls of the pipe, so it is pushed out through the hole. (c) The sideways water pressure is very large near the bottom of the dam, so a broad base is needed to withstand it. (d) The water column above the ground-floor tap is taller, so the pressure there is greater.
s: (a) Taller water column, so more pressure and more bulge
(b) Water presses on the walls of the pipe and is pushed out of the hole
(c) Sideways pressure is largest near the bottom, so the base is broad to withstand it
(d) Taller column above the ground-floor tap gives more pressure there

questions.q: A balloon is tied to the lower end of a pipe that holds water to a height of 10 cm. Which change will make the balloon bulge more?
questions.a: Adding water to the same pipe until the column is 20 cm high
o: Adding water to the same pipe until the column is 20 cm high
Moving the water into a wider pipe, where it stands lower
Using a much wider pipe that is also filled to a height of 10 cm
Pouring out half the water so the pipe is lighter to hold

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with the idea it shows in Column II.
Column I: I. Balloons at the ends of a wide pipe and a narrow pipe, filled to the same height, bulge equally.  II. Water flows out of holes made around the sides of a bottle.  III. The base of a dam is much broader than its top.  IV. An overhead tank is fixed high on a building.
Column II: A. The sideways pressure of water is very large near the bottom.  B. The pressure at the taps grows with the height of the water column.  C. Liquids press on the walls of their container.  D. The bulge depends on the height of the column, not on the weight of the water.
questions.a: I-D, II-C, III-A, IV-B
o: I-D, II-C, III-A, IV-B
I-B, II-C, III-A, IV-D

I-C, II-D, III-A, IV-B

questions.q: A narrow glass jar and a wide steel pot are filled with water to exactly the same height. The water pressure at the bottom of the jar is 1500 Pa. The base of the jar has an area of 0.02 m2 and the base of the pot has an area of 0.06 m2. (a) What is the water pressure at the bottom of the pot? (b) Find the total force the water exerts on the base of each vessel. (c) Mohan says: 'The pot holds more water, so the pressure at its bottom must be larger.' Explain what is wrong with his idea.
questions.a: (a) 1500 Pa, the same as in the jar, because the water stands to the same height in both. (b) Force = Pressure x Area: jar 1500 x 0.02 = 30 N; pot 1500 x 0.06 = 90 N. (c) Liquid pressure depends on the height of the column, not on the amount or weight of water. The pot has more water, so the total force on its larger base is larger (90 N against 30 N), but the pressure is the same.
s: (a) States 1500 Pa, equal because the heights are equal
(b) Uses Force = Pressure x Area to get 30 N and 90 N
(c) Explains that pressure depends on height only; more water gives more force on a larger base, not more pressure

questions.q:
A hill village in Uttarakhand gets water from one storage tank on the slope above it. The table gives how far the water surface in the tank is above each tap: temple tap 3 m, shop tap 5 m, school tap 8 m, clinic tap 12 m. The temple committee says its tap needs the water surface to be at least 6 m above it to give a good stream. The council can either (i) raise the tank 3 m higher up the slope, or (ii) move the temple tap 2.5 m lower down the slope.
(a) Which tap gets the strongest stream? Give a reason.
(b) Arrange the four taps from the lowest water pressure to the highest.
(c) A crack in the side of the pipe near the clinic sprays water outwards. What property of liquid pressure does this show?
(d) Which plan, (i) or (ii), meets the temple's need? Show your working.
questions.a: (a) The clinic tap, because the water column above it is the tallest (12 m) and liquid pressure increases with the height of the column. (b) Temple (3 m), shop (5 m), school (8 m), clinic (12 m). (c) Liquids exert pressure in all directions, including sideways on the walls of the pipe. (d) Plan (i): raising the tank 3 m makes the height above the temple tap 3 + 3 = 6 m, which meets the 6 m need. Plan (ii) gives only 3 + 2.5 = 5.5 m, which is less than 6 m. So the council should raise the tank.
s: (a) Names the clinic tap: tallest water column gives the greatest pressure
(b) Orders temple, shop, school, clinic
(c) States that liquids exert pressure in all directions, including on the walls of the pipe
(d) Finds 6 m for plan (i) and 5.5 m for plan (ii), and chooses raising the tank

questions.q: A school weather club in Bhopal records the air pressure as 100600 Pa at 8 a.m. and as 1003 hPa at 4 p.m. (1 hPa = 1 mb = 100 Pa) (a) Write the 8 a.m. reading in hectopascals. (b) By how many hectopascals did the pressure fall during the day? (c) Write this fall in pascals and in millibars.
s: (a) Converts 100600 Pa to 1006 hPa
(b) Finds a fall of 3 hPa

questions.q: True or False? 'A rubber sucker sticks to a smooth tile because the air trapped inside its cup is at a higher pressure than the air outside.' Give the verdict and the correct explanation.
questions.a: False. Pressing the sucker pushes most of the air out of its cup, so the pressure inside is reduced. The sucker sticks because the pressure of the air outside is higher than the pressure inside.
s: States False
Explains that air is pushed out, so the inside pressure is lower and the higher outside pressure holds the sucker

questions.q: The air column above a small patch of our skin presses on it with a very large force, yet we are not crushed. (a) Suppose the pressure inside a person's body were much lower than the atmospheric pressure outside. What would the outside air do to the body? (b) What keeps this from happening normally, and what causes the pressure inside the body? (c) Name one activity in the chapter in which a low pressure inside and a higher pressure outside make an object press hard against a surface.
questions.a: (a) The outside pressure would not be balanced, so the air would push the body inwards and squeeze or crush it. (b) Normally the pressure inside our body is equal to the atmospheric pressure, so it balances the pressure from outside. The pressure inside is caused by the movement of fluids and gases in the tissues and organs. (c) The rubber sucker: pressing it pushes out the air from its cup, so the higher outside air pressure holds it firmly to the surface.
s: (a) Predicts the unbalanced outside pressure would push the body inwards and crush it
(b) States the inside pressure equals atmospheric pressure, caused by fluids and gases moving in tissues and organs
(c) Names the rubber sucker and links it to lower pressure inside and higher pressure outside

questions.q: Between two regions, in which direction does air move?
questions.a: From the region of high air pressure to the region of low air pressure
o: From the region of high air pressure to the region of low air pressure
From the region of low air pressure to the region of high air pressure
From any region to any other region, whatever their air pressures
Only upwards, from the ground to the region of high air pressure

questions.q: Why does a sea breeze blow from the sea towards the land during the day?
questions.a: The land heats faster, so the warm air over it rises and leaves a low-pressure area that air from the sea moves into.
o: The land heats faster, so the warm air over it rises and leaves a low-pressure area that air from the sea moves into.
The sea heats faster, so the warm air over it rises and the higher pressure over the sea pushes it onto the land directly.
The land heats faster, so the warm air over it sinks and leaves a high-pressure area that pulls in air from the sea.
The sea and the land heat equally, so the air simply drifts from the larger region to the smaller one.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): On a sunny afternoon, the breeze at a beach blows from the land towards the sea.

questions.a: A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) In which direction does a land breeze blow? (b) Why does it blow at night?
questions.a: (a) From the land towards the sea. (b) At night the water is warmer than the land, so a low-pressure area develops above the sea, and air moves from the higher pressure over the land to the lower pressure over the sea.
s: (a) States that a land breeze blows from the land to the sea
(b) Explains that the sea is warmer at night, so low pressure forms over the sea and air moves to it from the land

questions.q: Give the reason for each, using what you know about the speed of air and air pressure. (a) When you blow into the gap between two hanging balloons, they move towards each other. (b) When you blow harder into the gap, they come together faster. (c) A weak roof can be lifted off when a high-speed wind blows over a closed house.
questions.a: (a) Blowing creates fast-moving air and a low-pressure area between the balloons, so the higher air pressure on their outer sides pushes them together. (b) Faster air between them means an even lower pressure there, so the pressure difference is larger and they move together faster. (c) The high-speed wind lowers the pressure above the roof, so the pressure inside the house is higher than above the roof; if this difference is large and the roof is weak, the roof is pushed up and blown away.
s: (a) Fast air makes low pressure between the balloons; higher outside pressure pushes them together
(b) Faster air gives still lower pressure, a bigger difference and faster movement
(c) Lower pressure above the roof than inside pushes a weak roof up

questions.q: On a hot summer afternoon, flags on poles along the beach at Puri flutter in the breeze. Which way do the flags point?
questions.a: Towards the land, since the breeze blows from the sea onto the land
o: Towards the land, since the breeze blows from the sea onto the land
Towards the sea, since the breeze blows from the land out to the sea
Towards the sea, since warm air over the land pushes out over the water

questions.q: True or False? 'On a sunny day, the air pressure over the sea is lower than the air pressure over the land.' Give the verdict and the correct explanation.
questions.a: False. During the day the land heats faster, so the air above it becomes warmer and lighter and rises, creating low pressure over the land. The pressure over the sea is higher, which is why the sea breeze blows from the sea to the land.

questions.q: Sanjana joins an inflated balloon P, in which the air pressure is 104000 Pa, by a straw to a balloon Q, in which the air pressure is 101000 Pa. (a) In which direction does the air flow through the straw, and why? (b) What happens to the sizes of the two balloons? (c) When does the air stop flowing? (d) In a second set-up she joins an identical balloon at 104000 Pa to a balloon R at 103000 Pa. At the start, will the air flow faster or slower than it did from P to Q? Give a reason using the pressure differences.
questions.a: (a) From P to Q, because air moves from a region of higher pressure (104000 Pa) to lower pressure (101000 Pa). (b) P becomes smaller and Q becomes bigger. (c) When the pressures in the two balloons become equal; they are then almost the same size. (d) Slower: the pressure difference is now 104000 - 103000 = 1000 Pa against 104000 - 101000 = 3000 Pa before, and the speed of the moving air is higher when the pressure difference is higher.
s: (a) Air flows from P to Q, from higher to lower pressure
(b) P shrinks and Q swells
(c) The flow stops when the two pressures become equal
(d) Finds differences of 3000 Pa and 1000 Pa and concludes the flow is slower

questions.q:
Fishermen at a village near Ratnagiri use small sailing boats, which go fastest when the wind blows from behind them. A school weather club near the shore took these readings on a clear summer day. At 5 a.m.: land 22 C, sea surface 26 C. At 3 p.m.: land 35 C, sea surface 29 C. The fishermen go out to sea once a day and return the same day.
(a) At 3 p.m., is the air pressure lower over the land or over the sea? Give a reason.
(b) In which direction does the breeze blow at 3 p.m.?
(c) In which direction does the breeze blow at 5 a.m.? Use the readings.
(d) Using your answers, decide when the fishermen should set out and when they should sail back. Justify your decision.
questions.a: (a) Over the land: at 3 p.m. the land (35 C) is hotter than the sea (29 C), so the warm, light air over the land rises and leaves a low-pressure area there. (b) From the sea to the land (a sea breeze). (c) At 5 a.m. the sea (26 C) is warmer than the land (22 C), so the low pressure is over the sea and the breeze blows from the land to the sea (a land breeze). (d) They should set out early in the morning, when the land breeze blows out to sea behind them, and sail back in the afternoon, when the sea breeze blows towards the land behind them.
s: (a) Low pressure over the land, because the hotter land's air rises
(b) Sea to land
(c) Land to sea, since the sea is warmer at 5 a.m.
(d) Decides to leave early morning with the land breeze and return in the afternoon with the sea breeze

questions.q: On a sunny afternoon at Kovalam beach, a cool breeze blows from the sea onto the sand. Explain this step by step and then make a prediction. (a) Which gets heated faster during the day, the land or the sea? (b) What happens to the air above the land, and why? (c) Where is the air pressure higher and where is it lower? (d) Why does this make the breeze blow from the sea? (e) On one cloudy day the land and the sea stay at the same temperature all day. Predict whether a sea breeze would blow that afternoon, and give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The land. (b) The air above the land becomes warmer and lighter, so it rises. (c) Rising air leaves low pressure over the land; the pressure over the sea is higher. (d) Air moves from a region of high pressure to a region of low pressure, so air from over the sea flows onto the land as a sea breeze. (e) No sea breeze would be expected: with equal temperatures there is no extra rising air over the land, so no pressure difference between land and sea is set up, and without a pressure difference there is no such breeze.
s: (a) Land heats faster
(b) Air over the land becomes warmer and lighter and rises
(c) Low pressure over the land, higher over the sea
(d) Air moves from high to low pressure, so it blows from sea to land
(e) Predicts no sea breeze because equal temperatures give no pressure difference

questions.q: A group of hikers is caught in a thunderstorm with lightning in an open field near Nashik. Using the safety advice in the chapter, write what they should do in each case. (a) A tall tree stands in the middle of the field. (b) How should they position themselves on the ground? (c) One hiker wants to lie down flat on the grass. (d) Another hiker is carrying an umbrella with a metallic rod. (e) Two hikers are wading in a stream at the edge of the field.
questions.a: (a) Stay away from the tall tree, as one must keep away from tall objects. (b) Find a low-lying open area and crouch down, keeping contact with the ground as small as possible. (c) Do not lie down flat. (d) Do not use the umbrella with a metallic rod. (e) Get out of the water.
s: (a) Keep away from the tall tree (tall objects)
(b) Crouch down in a low-lying open area with as little contact with the ground as possible
(c) Do not lie down flat
(d) Avoid using the umbrella with a metallic rod
(e) Get out of the water

questions.q:
On an April afternoon, the temperature at a coffee estate in Kodagu, Karnataka, reaches 37 C and the air is very humid. By 4 p.m. tall dark clouds have built up. Strong winds start blowing, heavy rain falls, and bright flashes of light are each followed by loud bangs. Most workers are in the open plantation; one of them has taken shelter under a tall silver oak tree.
(a) According to the chapter, do such local thunderstorms in Karnataka help or harm the coffee plants?
(b) Why are storms like this more frequent in a country like India?
(c) What produces the loud bangs heard after the flashes?
(d) What should the worker under the tall tree do, and how should he wait out the storm?
questions.a: (a) They help: local thunderstorms in Karnataka help in the growth of coffee plants. (b) Storms are more frequent in hot, humid, tropical regions like India, where heated, moist air rises and forms storm clouds. (c) Lightning rapidly heats the air around it, so the air expands and produces the loud sound called thunder. (d) He should move away from the tall tree, go to a low-lying open area and crouch down, keeping contact with the ground small; he should not lie down flat.
s: (a) States that they help the growth of coffee plants
(b) Hot, humid, tropical regions like India have more storms
(c) Lightning heats the air, which expands and makes thunder
(d) Move away from the tall tree and crouch in a low-lying open area, not lying flat

questions.q:
Read these statements about thunderstorms.
I. Lightning can occur only between a cloud and the ground.
II. Normally air acts as an electrical insulator and does not let opposite charges meet.
III. Kalboishakhi thunderstorms occur after the monsoon has ended.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II only
o: II only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: Explain the part each of these plays in producing a thunderstorm with lightning. (a) A large amount of moisture in the warm air rising from heated land. (b) Warm air rising to such great heights that it becomes very cold there. (c) Strong winds blowing upwards and downwards inside the cloud.
questions.a: (a) As the moist air rises it expands and cools, and its moisture condenses into droplets that form clouds; the droplets merge into heavier drops that fall as rain. (b) The low temperature at great heights turns some water droplets into ice particles. (c) These winds make the ice particles and water droplets rub against each other, so static electric charges develop: the lighter, positively charged ice particles go to the top of the cloud and the heavier, negatively charged droplets stay at the bottom. This charge separation leads to lightning.
s: (a) Moisture condenses in the cooling rising air to form clouds and rain
(b) Very low temperature turns water droplets into ice particles
(c) Up-and-down winds rub ice and droplets together, separating positive (top) and negative (bottom) charges

questions.q: True or False? 'Some local thunderstorms in India are useful to farmers.' Give the verdict and support it with an example from the chapter.
questions.a: True. Local thunderstorms such as Kalboishakhi (West Bengal, Bihar, Jharkhand) and Bordoisila (Assam) come before the monsoon and help kharif crops to grow; mango showers in Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu support the ripening of mangoes.
s: States True
Gives a correct example: Kalboishakhi or Bordoisila helping kharif crops, mango showers ripening mangoes, or coffee in Karnataka

questions.q: Which situation leads to a flash of lightning between a storm cloud and the ground below it?
questions.a: The cloud's lower part and the ground carry opposite charges that build up until the insulating property of air breaks down.
o: The cloud's lower part and the ground carry opposite charges that build up until the insulating property of air breaks down.
The cloud's lower part and the ground carry the same kind of charge, which builds up until the air begins to conduct easily.
The cloud's lower part becomes positively charged and is pulled down towards the negatively charged ground below it.
Heavy rain soaks the ground, and the wet air then carries the charges from the falling raindrops down to the earth.

questions.q: Where do cyclones form?
questions.a: Over warm ocean waters
o: Over warm ocean waters
Over heated land far from any sea
Over cold ocean waters near the poles
Over high, snow-covered mountains

questions.q: What is the region of lowest pressure at the centre of a cyclone called?
questions.a: The eye of the cyclone
o: The eye of the cyclone
The storm surge
The sea breeze
The lightning conductor

questions.q:
Assertion (A): As a cyclone builds up over the ocean, the moist air in it keeps rising higher and the pressure at its centre becomes even lower.
Reason (R): When water vapour condenses into raindrops, heat is released, which further warms the rising air.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What is a cyclone? (b) Why does a cyclone gradually lose its strength after it reaches land?
questions.a: (a) A cyclone is a large spinning system of clouds, winds and rain that forms over warm ocean waters, with a very low-pressure area at its centre and high-speed winds around it. (b) Over land, its source of moist air is cut off, so it gradually loses strength.
s: (a) Describes a cyclone as a spinning system of clouds, winds and rain formed over warm ocean water
(b) States that over land the source of moist air is cut off

questions.q: A family lives in a cyclone-prone village on the coast of Andhra Pradesh. Give one reason for each of these steps suggested in the chapter. (a) Staying updated on weather reports, alerts and warnings from the India Meteorological Department (IMD). (b) Keeping an emergency kit with essential items ready. (c) Moving quickly to a nearby designated cyclone shelter during a cyclone.
questions.a: (a) Cyclones are tracked by weather satellites and their path can be predicted, so IMD warnings give the family time to prepare and reduce harm to life and property. (b) Roads may be blocked and power may be cut for days, so essential items must already be at hand. (c) Houses near the coast can be hit by very strong winds and flooded by the surge of seawater, so a designated shelter keeps the family safer.
s: (a) IMD warnings, based on tracking the cyclone's path, give time to prepare and reduce harm
(b) Blocked roads and long power cuts mean essentials must be ready in advance
(c) A designated shelter protects against strong winds and flooding

questions.q: Air pressure is measured at four points along a straight line across a cyclone, one of them at its centre: K 1004 hPa, L 996 hPa, M 982 hPa and N 1000 hPa. At which point is the wind most likely to be calm?
questions.a: M, because the lowest pressure is at the eye, where the wind is calm
o: M, because the lowest pressure is at the eye, where the wind is calm
K, because the highest pressure is at the eye, where the wind is calm
L, because the strongest winds and calm air are found together
N, because the wind is calm wherever the pressure is close to 1000 hPa

questions.q: A cyclone has crossed the coast and is now 100 km inland. Raju says: 'Now that it is over land, it has lost its supply of moist air, so it can no longer do any harm to the villages in its path.' (a) What part of Raju's statement is correct? (b) What part is wrong? Use the chapter. (c) Give your overall verdict on his claim.
questions.a: (a) Correct: over land the source of moist air is cut off and the cyclone loses strength. (b) Wrong: it loses strength only gradually, and while travelling over land it still leaves a trail of destruction; its heavy rain can make rivers overflow and trigger landslides. (c) Raju is only partly right; the villages in its path must still follow the warnings and stay safe.
s: (a) Agrees that over land the moist air supply is cut off and it weakens
(b) Points out it weakens gradually and its rain can still cause floods, landslides and destruction
(c) Concludes that the claim is only partly right

questions.q: The chapter says that under certain conditions a storm may develop into a cyclone. Compare an ordinary storm and a cyclone under these four heads, using only what the chapter says. (a) Where the warm, moist air that feeds it rises from. (b) Which one produces higher wind speeds. (c) Which one has a calm centre of lowest pressure, and what surrounds that centre. (d) Which one can push a wall of seawater onto the coast, and how.
questions.a: (a) A storm forms when land gets heated and the warm, moist air above it rises; a cyclone forms over warm ocean waters, where the warm, moist air above the heated water rises. (b) A cyclone: as it moves from the ocean towards land it generates higher wind speeds than regular thunderstorms. (c) A cyclone: its centre, the eye, has the lowest pressure and calm wind, and the region around it has strong winds and heavy rainfall. (d) A cyclone: its strong winds push ocean water towards the shore, creating a wall of water that can be 3-12 metres high and can flood coastal areas.
s: (a) Storm from heated land; cyclone from warm ocean water
(b) Cyclone produces higher wind speeds than regular thunderstorms
(c) Cyclone has a calm eye of lowest pressure surrounded by strong winds and heavy rain
(d) Cyclone winds push ocean water to the shore as a 3-12 m wall of water

questions.q:
On the same April afternoon, a weather office studies two systems. System P is over the Bay of Bengal, 350 km from the Odisha coast and moving towards it. Its pressure is 975 hPa at the centre and 1005 hPa at its outer edge, its winds reach 190 km/h, and a spinning band of clouds surrounds a calm centre. System Q is over the hot Bihar plains: its lowest pressure is 1001 hPa, gusts reach 70 km/h, it brings lightning and hail, it has no calm centre, and it lasts about two hours.
(a) Which system is a cyclone? Give two features from the data that show it.
(b) Find the pressure difference between the centre and the edge of System P, in hPa and in Pa (1 hPa = 100 Pa).
(c) What will happen to the strength of System P after it crosses the coast, and why?
(d) The office must send one main safety message to each region. What should it tell people on the Odisha coast, and what should it tell people in Bihar? Justify each.
questions.a: (a) System P: it formed over warm ocean water, it is a spinning system with a calm centre (an eye) of very low pressure, and its winds are far stronger. (b) 1005 - 975 = 30 hPa, which is 30 x 100 = 3000 Pa. (c) It will gradually lose strength, because over land its source of moist air is cut off; but it can still cause destruction while it weakens. (d) Odisha coast: follow IMD warnings, keep emergency kits ready and move to designated cyclone shelters, because P brings very strong winds, a storm surge and flooding. Bihar: follow lightning safety, such as keeping away from tall objects, crouching in a low-lying open area and getting out of water, because Q is a thunderstorm with lightning.
s: (a) Names P, citing two of: forms over warm ocean, spins round a calm eye, very low centre pressure, very strong winds
(b) Finds 30 hPa and 3000 Pa
(c) Says it weakens gradually over land because the moist air supply is cut off
(d) Cyclone shelter, kit and IMD warnings for Odisha; lightning precautions for Bihar, each justified

questions.q: A cyclone needs several things to happen together. Predict what would happen in each imagined case, and give the reason from the chapter. (a) The ocean water below the air stays cold instead of getting heated. (b) The water vapour in the rising air condenses into raindrops, but no heat is released when it does. (c) The Earth stopped rotating. (d) Weather monitoring satellites did not exist. (e) From your answers to (a) to (c), name the three conditions that together build a cyclone.
questions.a: (a) No cyclone would form: there would be no warm, moist air rising from the heated ocean to start the low-pressure area. (b) The rising air would not get the extra warming that makes it rise further, so the pressure would not drop as low and the system would not build up into a cyclone. (c) The air rushing in would still rise, but it would not be made to spin, so there would be no spinning system of clouds, winds and rain, which is what a cyclone is. (d) Cyclones could not be tracked and their path predicted in time, so warnings would come late and the harm to life and property would be greater. (e) Warm ocean water giving warm, moist rising air; heat released when the water vapour condenses; and the Earth's rotation making the moving air spin.
s: (a) No cyclone, since no warm moist air rises from cold water
(b) No extra warming from condensation, so the pressure does not drop enough for the system to build up
(c) The inflowing air would not spin, so no spinning cyclone
(d) No tracking or prediction of the path, so later warnings and more harm
(e) Names warm ocean water, heat from condensation and the Earth's rotation
